title: the Sri Yantra
hook: trace one triangle at the yantra's heart, and it won't come apart
tomorrow: a dot at the very center. who gets to walk all the way in?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Yantra's lotuses: three circles, sixteen petals, then eight, a throne rising out of the mud and opening toward the center. Today, what sits on that throne.

Try this with any picture of the Sri Yantra. Put a fingertip on one corner of a triangle at its heart and trace just that one triangle. The line runs off, crosses another, then another, and within seconds there's no telling which shape you started on. Every triangle is cut by others, and the cuts make new, smaller triangles. Odd, for a drawing someone made with such care. Why draw shapes that refuse to come apart?
screen: `TRACE ONE TRIANGLE.` → `THE LINES RUN OFF.` → `WHY WON'T THEY COME APART?`

segments.voice: The Saundarya Lahari, the hymn that has been counting the yantra, reaches this tangle and names it. Four triangles, it says, belong to Shiva, and five to Shakti, the Goddess as power. Nine in all, and the verse calls them root natures, the ground everything else grows out of. In the usual drawing, some point up and some point down, and some teachers read the upward ones as Shiva and the downward ones as Shakti. Now put that next to what your fingertip found. The triangles of Shiva and the triangles of Shakti aren't drawn side by side, like two separate pictures. They're woven through each other, so tightly you can't lift one out without tearing the rest. That's the answer to the puzzle. In Sri Vidya, Shiva and Shakti aren't two beings who happen to meet now and then. They're held together, awareness and power, and the world comes from their meeting. The yantra doesn't argue for it. It draws it, and lets the eye get lost in it. And the small triangles made where the lines cross? Some teachers say each one is a home for a goddess honored in worship. So the tangle isn't empty. It's crowded, full of presence. Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: in this drawing, you can't put a finger on Shiva without touching Shakti too.
screen: `FOUR OF SHIVA, FIVE OF SHAKTI.` · `NINE ROOT NATURES.` · `WOVEN, NOT SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE CROSSINGS ARE FULL.` · then, large: `TWO THAT WON'T COME APART.`

segments.voice: Lace your fingers together loosely in your lap, so it's hard to tell where one hand stops and the other starts. Let the breath be slow and even, and keep your attention on the place where the fingers weave. Don't pull them apart; just rest there.
The Sri Yantra, at its heart: nine triangles, four of Shiva and five of Shakti, woven so neither stands alone.
Hold onto this: the Sri Yantra, two woven so tightly they won't come apart. Day sixteen thirty-three.

screen: `DAY 1633 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO GETS TO WALK ALL THE WAY IN?`

options: the triangles of Shiva and Shakti, woven so neither stands alone.
the outer square, where each gate stands apart from the others.
the lotus rings, each petal drawn separate and complete.
fork.reveal: four triangles of Shiva and five of Shakti, woven so tightly none can be lifted out: in Sri Vidya, awareness and power held together.

options: not hopeless: four of Shiva, five of Shakti, woven so neither can be lifted out.

kind of. it's nine copies of one triangle, and each means the same thing.
